outline.description: Sets the factual and procedural foundation of United States v. Constantinescu, explaining the alleged pump‑and‑dump scheme, the charges filed, the district court's dismissal, and the appellate review.
subtopics: The alleged pump‑and‑dump scheme on social‑media platforms
Count of conspiracy and securities‑fraud charges (18 U.S.C. §§ 1349, 1348)
Outcome in district court: dismissal for failure to allege deprivation of property
The government’s timely appeal and the standard of review for indictment sufficiency

outline.description: Explains the Fifth Circuit’s de novo approach to evaluating whether an indictment states an offense, including the elements an indictment must allege and the relevant precedential authorities.
subtopics: De novo review of indictment sufficiency (United States v. Rafoi)
Three statutory requirements: element enumeration, fair notice, double‑jeopardy protection
Key Fifth Circuit cases defining indictment adequacy (Gaytan, Guzman‑Ocampo)
Interaction with the Rule 7(b) elements of the federal criminal code

outline.chapter_title: Statutory Framework: Securities Fraud and Its Relationship to Wire/Fraud Statutes
outline.description: Analyzes 18 U.S.C. § 1348, its borrowed concepts from mail‑ and wire‑fraud statutes, and the two core elements—scheme to defraud and intent to defraud.
subtopics: Text of § 1348 and its “scheme to defraud” and “intent to defraud” requirements
Borrowed definitions from 18 U.S.C. §§ 1341‑1343
The material‑misrepresentation and fraudulent‑inducement theories
Circuit precedent interpreting these elements (Greenlaw, Evans)

outline.chapter_title: Supreme Court Guidance: Ciminelli and Kousisis
outline.description: Summarizes the Supreme Court’s recent decisions distinguishing the right‑to‑control theory from the fraudulent‑inducement theory and clarifies that economic loss is not required for a fraud conviction.
subtopics: Ciminelli: rejection of the right‑to‑control theory and protection of traditional property interests
Definition of “traditional property interest” vs. valuable economic information
Kousisis: affirmation of the fraudulent‑inducement theory and the irrelevance of victim’s net loss
How these decisions shape the analysis of scheme and intent in Constantinescu

outline.chapter_title: Court’s Application of Law to the Facts
outline.description: Details the Fifth Circuit’s reasoning that the indictment adequately alleges a scheme to defraud and an intent to defraud, rebutting the defendants’ arguments with the Supreme Court precedent.
subtopics: Why the indictment goes beyond depriving followers of information— it alleges fraudulent purchase of securities
Application of the fraudulent‑inducement theory to the social‑media “pump” conduct
Analysis of intent: profit motive satisfies “intent to obtain money or property” regardless of victim loss
Rejection of the defendants’ “no property interest” and “no victim harm” arguments

outline.description: Outlines the appellate court’s disposition, the remand instructions, and the implications for future securities‑fraud prosecutions involving modern communication platforms.
subtopics: Reversal of the district court’s dismissal and remand for further proceedings
Practical effect on indictment drafting for online‑based fraud schemes
Potential impact on prosecutorial strategy and defense arguments in the Fifth Circuit
Relation to ongoing evolution of fraud jurisprudence post‑Ciminelli/Kousisis
